children: Vinod Mahanta Mumbai: Audit committees and management teams at India's largest companies have started preparing for a major change in financial reporting under Ind AS 118, a proposed accounting standard that could alter the manner in which companies report operating profit, classify income and expenses, and communicate financial performance to investors.

The standard is likely to have implications for finance information systems, internal controls and financial performance indicators used by the management. Ind AS 118 is currently awaiting notification by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Changes to Schedule III of the Companies Act, which governs financial statement formats, are also expected.

India has proposed implementation from April 1, 2027, for annual reporting periods beginning on or after that date, while IFRS 18 takes effect on January 1, 2027. Companies have begun discussing transition plans, though their levels of preparedness vary, said Samir Shah, audit leader at Deloitte Haskins & Sells. "The transition to IFRS 18 is increasingly becoming a boardroom issue," he said. Ketan Dalal, who chairs the audit committees of Zensar Technologies, Torrent Power and HDFC Life said, "Its objective is to improve comparability and comprehension.

But in today's challenging business environment, the transition will put considerable pressure on companies and audit committees." The lack of final rules and reporting formats is complicating preparations, with companies reluctant to commit to systems changes before the requirements are settled. Currently, companies report expenses by nature.

The new standard permits operating expenses by nature, function or both, depending on what provides users the most useful information, aligning India's reporting rules more closely with global standards. "The biggest topic of discussion for corporates is whether the new requirements will result in a shift towards function-wise presentation" said Abhishek Rara, Partner at Price Waterhouse. "For many entities that may need to adopt this presentation, the change could require significant modifications to their processes and ERP systems.," he added. Under functional reporting, expenses are classified by the activities they support, such as cost of sales, distribution, research and development, sales and marketing, and general and administrative expenses.

Employee benefits and depreciation, currently reported by nature, may need to be allocated across functions. Companies present a 'gross margin' subtotal under this approach. The exercise could prove complex for companies whose cost-centre structures do not support functional allocations, requiring finance teams to work with technology, human resources.

title: Ind AS 118: Big Changes to Financial Reporting Soon
